job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Vera, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior drawing technician at a small surveying and civil design firm in Dunmore, since August. I finished a civil engineering degree in June, with one summer placement at a road contractor. Most days I clean up site survey drawings, check levels against the engineer's notes and print sets for the site team. I share a damp flat with two housemates, and my student loan letter sits unopened on the shelf. I like being on a site visit once a fortnight, and I hate the Sunday-night feeling about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means nobody gets thrown out for a machine. At work I'd probably say little, since our boss Marek likes to hear that everything is fine. To my friends from uni I'd say the hype was always about shares and not about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still doesn't make me feel safe. My pay is low, my loan takes a chunk each month and my savings wouldn't cover a month of rent. A slow AI world is the same stress I have now, just with less news about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the drawings by hand in the software we already have, and I'd ask Marek for the site-inspection course the firm sometimes pays for. I'd also start putting 30 pounds a month into a savings account, which is all I can spare. I wouldn't touch AI tools, because I've never trusted them near a drawing someone could build from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired more than scared. It's a flat feeling, like walking uphill on a road that never ends. I'd be relieved that nothing is changing, but relieved isn't the same as comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm might lose a client. Which bill would you cut first, and who could help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if the firm lost a client? Probably my phone plan and the gym, then I'd skip the train and walk 40 minutes to work. The rent and the loan can't move, so I'd be eating pasta for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your feeling of being behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who would help? Nobody in my family has money, my mum cleans offices and my dad is on disability. I have to be the one who doesn't fall, because I can't ask anyone to catch me.

say: I'd tell my friends this is **good news**, since nobody loses a job to a machine.
At work I'd keep quiet, because my boss likes hearing that **everything is fine**.
think: My **money** worries stay the same, with low pay, a big loan and almost no savings.
Slow AI doesn't make me feel safe, because my **debt** is the real problem.
do: Ask my boss to pay for the **site-inspection course** the firm sometimes funds.
Put **30 pounds** a month into a savings account.
Skip AI tools and keep drawing in the **current software**.
feel: I feel **tired**, like walking uphill on a road that never ends.
S0.quote: The rent and the loan can't move, so I'd be eating pasta for a while.
fieldNote: Vera sounds flat rather than frightened, and her worry is **debt** more than technology.
She trusts only what a person has checked and refuses AI near a drawing someone could build from.
Her family can't help, so every plan rests on her own small savings.

steps.text: Keep drawing site layouts in the firm's current software
Ask Marek to pay for the site-inspection course
Put 30 pounds a month into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what happens when companies decide people are a cost. Checking, drawing and planning are exactly what a junior like me does, so the firm will say it needs fewer juniors. I'd want the union and the government to step in before the first redundancy letter, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm one of the first. Marek already told me the next graduate hire is on hold, and my job is half checking levels and half tidying drawings, which software can do. I'm afraid I'll be told I'm replaced just as my loan payments get bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the engineers' union this month, which costs 12 pounds, and go to the meeting about junior jobs. I'd take every site visit I can, because standing in a trench is the part a machine isn't doing yet. I'd also look at a surveying certificate in the evenings, but only if the firm pays half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Angry, if I'm honest, and then guilty for being angry. I did everything I was told, a good degree and a placement, and now the ground moves under me. I don't blame the software, I blame the people who decide to use it to cut wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your housemate Sana's call centre. What did you learn from watching her team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My housemate Sana works in a call centre, and her team got cut by half last year. She says the first thing they did was stop answering new-hire questions, so nobody learned anything. I'm scared the same thing will happen to graduates in drawing offices, where we learn by doing the boring work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to move, what would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The most useful thing would be a rule that firms keep training juniors, like an apprenticeship with real pay. Without that, I'd make a plan to move to a bigger city, but I can't afford the deposit for a room there.

say: I'd say firms are using AI as an excuse to **cut juniors** and wages.
I'd push for the **union** and the government to act before layoffs, not after.
think: I think I'm among the **first to go**, because half my job is checking and tidying drawings.
I blame the **decision-makers**, not the software, and I feel guilty for being so angry.
do: Join the engineers' **union** for 12 pounds and go to the junior-jobs meeting.
Volunteer for every **site visit**, since fieldwork is harder to automate.
Ask the firm to pay half of an evening **surveying certificate**.
feel: I feel **angry**, then guilty, because I did everything I was told.
S1.quote: I did everything I was told, a good degree and a placement, and now the ground moves under me.
fieldNote: Vera blames **employers** and sees collective action as her main protection, which fits her progressive views.
Her fear is concrete: the next graduate hire is already on hold.
She guards herself against AI tools, yet is clear about what in her job software could take.

steps.text: Join the engineers' union and go to the junior-jobs meeting
Volunteer for site visits to learn the fieldwork
Write to my local representative about funded junior apprenticeships
Cut the gym and walk to work to save money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency rules this year, before it's too late. Two years isn't enough for a country to rebuild how people earn. I'd tell everyone at the union meeting that they should be demanding a guaranteed income now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job is gone before my loan is paid. Drawings, calculations and design checking are all thinking work, and AI would do them in minutes. The robots for site work come later, but I'm not a bricklayer and I never learned to be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd empty my small savings into rent for as many months as it covers, then ask for help from the council. I'd go to every union and community meeting, because I think only a crowd gets anything. I'd also consider leaving my flat to share a room with my mum, and I hate saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and a bit numb. I'd lie awake adding up my loan and my rent. I'd feel angry at the companies that can switch this on in two years and at governments that watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first in the weeks after you heard it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do I have a plan beyond that? No. I'd keep going to work as long as the firm keeps me, and take what I can learn about site safety. I can't make a plan for a world nobody has described yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd consider a hands-on trade. Is that something you'd really do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone offered a retraining for a hands-on trade like electrical installation, I'd take it, even though I told myself I'd never be on a ladder. But I'd want it paid for, because I can't pay rent and a course.

say: I'd say we need **emergency rules** this year, because two years is too short.
I'd demand a guaranteed **income** at the union meeting.
think: I think my job is **gone** before my student loan is paid.
Thinking work is what I do, and I never learned a **hands-on trade**.
do: Spend my small savings on **rent** for as many months as it covers.
Go to every **union** and community meeting to push for support.
Ask the council for **help** and consider moving back in with my mum.
feel: I feel **scared** and numb, lying awake adding up loan and rent.
S2.quote: I can't make a plan for a world nobody has described yet.
fieldNote: Vera has **no safety net**, and her plan is to hold the job as long as possible and push for public support.
Her anger points at companies and governments for moving too fast, not at the technology itself.
She admits she'd retrain in a hands-on trade if it were funded, which she had ruled out before.

steps.text: Go to every union and community meeting about jobs
Press my representative for a guaranteed income
Ask the council for housing help and move back with my mum
Stop buying anything except food and rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but I'd still say it needs a plan from the government now. I'd tell my colleagues to put pressure on the union to negotiate junior job protections. I'd be a bit less loud than with the two-year one, because there's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I have a window to make myself less replaceable. By 2031 my loan is smaller, and if I stay in the field I might have a trade certificate. The problem is that thinking AI comes first, so the desk parts of my job will disappear before I've got that certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train in site inspection and health and safety, the parts that need a person on the ground. I'd save 100 pounds a month once my pay improves and put the rest into the loan. I'd also keep going to union meetings, because the first years matter for who gets protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautious and a bit hopeful. Five years feels like seeing a storm over the hills and having time to bring the washing in. I still feel a lump in my chest about my loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly changes for you with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two is that I can pay the rent without panic. I'd still not trust it, because companies tend to say they'll wait and then they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum in that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum to keep her savings in a safe place and not lend me anything, because I don't want her taking a risk. That's the harder conversation, since she'd say yes.

say: I'd say the government needs a **plan now**, and the union should win junior job protections.
I'd be quieter than in the two-year world, because there's **room to breathe**.
think: I have a **window** to become harder to replace, if I use it well.
The desk parts of my job will vanish **first**, before any certificate I earn.
do: Train in **site inspection** and health and safety, the parts needing a person.
Save **100 pounds** a month once pay improves and put the rest on the loan.
Keep attending **union** meetings so juniors get protected.
feel: I feel **cautious** and a bit hopeful, like bringing the washing in before a storm.
S3.quote: Five years feels like seeing a storm over the hills and having time to bring the washing in.
fieldNote: Vera uses the extra time for **practical skills** rather than software, which matches her distrust of AI tools.
She still doubts companies will wait, so hope is limited.
Her mother's protection matters to her, and she'd rather carry risk herself.

steps.text: Study site inspection and health and safety in the evenings
Pay 100 pounds a month extra toward my student loan
Attend every union meeting and speak up for junior jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd say we should be planning properly, like a school curriculum for the change. I'd say it to friends and online, and I'd say the unions need to be ready. It's not a crisis yet, but it will be if no one starts now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, ten years means I'm 32 with a decent career if I stay careful. My loan will mostly be paid off by then. The risk is that I stay slow to pick up the new tools, and the world moves on without me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work my way up to a licensed role, like chartered engineer, which takes years of site work and signatures. I'd save for a flat deposit instead of renting forever, and I'd maybe learn one AI tool the firm already uses, to be able to say I've checked it. It would be the first time I try one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, to be honest. Not happy, but calm. Ten years gives my mum time to retire and my loan time to shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try one AI tool. What would make that feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I might never get comfortable with AI tools. A decade is long enough that not trusting them could cost me, and I know that. Maybe I'd have to let a colleague show me one at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the licensed route feel safer to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would help is the licensing route I mentioned. Chartered status is a person's name on a drawing, and that feels like a job that survives. I'd rather rely on that than on any promise from a company.

say: I'd say we should **plan properly** now, like a school curriculum for the change.
I'd tell friends the unions must be **ready** before it becomes a crisis.
think: Ten years could mean a **decent career** and a mostly paid-off loan at 32.
My real risk is staying **slow** with new tools while the world moves on.
do: Work toward a **chartered engineer** licence through site work and signatures.
Save for a flat **deposit** instead of renting forever.
Let a colleague show me one **AI tool** over lunch and test it.
feel: I feel **calm**, not happy, since ten years gives my loan time to shrink.
S4.quote: Chartered status is a person's name on a drawing, and that feels like a job that survives.
fieldNote: Vera is steadier here, but **uneasy** because her resistance to tools could cost her over a decade.
She trusts accountable human signatures and sees licensing as protection.
The first mention of trying an AI tool shows a small crack in her refusal.

steps.text: Work toward chartered engineer status through supervised site work
Save for a flat deposit instead of renting
Test one AI tool with a colleague over lunch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because my loan, my rent and no cushion all collide with a world that hasn't had time to react. What would help is a guaranteed income, funded retraining and a rule that firms keep taking on juniors. I don't want charity, just a fair chance to pay my way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are not the ones who made this decision. We got the degree, we did the placement, and we're being asked to carry the risk. I'd like decision-makers to remember that. I'm not afraid of the machine, I'm afraid of whoever decides to use it to make me cheaper.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the machine, I'm afraid of whoever decides to use it to make me cheaper.
portrait: Vera is a **civil engineering** graduate in her first job at a small drawing firm, with heavy student debt.
She distrusts **AI tools**, blames employers and decision-makers rather than technology, and puts faith in unions and public support.
Her family has no money to help, so every scenario is **her own savings** against her loan and rent.
She relaxes only when the timeline is long, and then turns to **licensing** and site skills.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world worries her most, because debt and rent meet a job that disappears with no time for help.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income**, paid retraining and a rule that firms keep taking on junior staff.
